title: Genomic characteristics of PD-L1-Induced resistance to EGFR-TKIs in lung adenocarcinoma
author: Guangming Yi; Fanghao Cai; Liangzhong Liu; Rongxin Liao; Xuan Jiang; Zhenzhou Yang; Xiaoyue Zhang
text:
ABSTRACT
Background
The co-occurrence of PD-L1 positivity and EGFR mutations in advanced NSCLC often limits EGFR-TKIs effectiveness, with unclear mechanisms.
Methods
We analyzed 103 treatment-naive EGFR-mutant LUAD patients from three centers, assessing PD-L1 expression and performing NGS analysis.
Results
SMO mutations and MET amplification were significantly higher in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group versus PD-L1 < 1% group (SMO: 8% vs. 0%, p = 0.048; MET: 18% vs. 7%, p = 0.023). The DNA Damage Response and Repair (DDR) pathogenic deficiency mutations, along with biological processes and signaling pathways related to DNA recombination, cell cycle transition and abnormal phosphorylation, were more prevalent in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group. PIK3CA and RARA clonal alterations were more common in PD-L1 < 1% group, while TP53 clonal mutations predominated in PD-L1 ≥ 1% group. Retrospective analysis showed EGFR-TKIs plus chemotherapy extended median PFS by 9.8 months, potentially overcoming EGFR-TKI monotherapy resistance.
Conclusion
This study elucidates the genomic characteristics of PD-L1-induced resistance to EGFR-TKIs. For patients with concurrent mutations in EGFR and PD-L1 expression, a first-line treatment strategy combining EGFR-TKIs with chemotherapy may offer a more effective alternative.
KEYWORDS: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1), drug resistance, chemotherapy
Plain Language Summary
This study looked at lung cancer patients who have two important characteristics: changes in a gene called EGFR and a protein called PD-L1. While there are drugs (EGFR-TKIs) that target EGFR mutations, they don’t always work well when PD-L1 is also present. The researchers studied 103 lung cancer patients to understand why this happens. They found that patients with higher PD-L1 levels had different genetic patterns, including more changes in genes that affect DNA repair and cell growth. Importantly, they discovered that combining standard EGFR-targeting drugs with chemotherapy helped patients respond better to treatment, extending the time before their cancer got worse by almost 10 months. This suggests that patients with both EGFR mutations and PD-L1 might benefit more from a combination treatment approach rather than using EGFR-targeting drugs alone.
1. Introduction
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most prevalent subtype. Among NSCLC cases, nearly half were lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) is a crucial driver gene, with a higher prevalence of mutations among Asians NSCLC, approximately 51%, and around 60% in LUAD cases [1]. NSCLC patients harboring activating EGFR mutation treated with EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) experience better clinical outcomes and fewer adverse effects compared to those undergoing systemic platinum-based chemotherapy [2]. Despite the majority of patients with sensitizing EGFR mutations responding positively, approximately 5–10% of patients exhibited intrinsic resistance to EGFR-TKIs [3]. The mechanism underlying primary resistance to EGFR-TKIs is not well understood and varies greatly among individuals. Beyond the established mechanisms involving c-MET amplification and de novo T790M mutations, additional factors such as ERBB2 amplification, PTEN loss, MYC amplification, BIM deletion polymorphism, and CRIPTO1 overexpression have been implicated [3,4].
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the Programmed Death-Receptor 1/Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) pathway have revolutionized the therapeutic management of advanced or metastatic NSCLC patients [5]. However, accumulating evidence indicates that the patients with co-occurrence of PD-L1-positive and activating EGFR mutations exhibit reduced efficacy of EGFR-TKIs [6–10]. Further stratification of patients with PD-L1 ≥ 1% into groups with PD-L1 1%-49% and ≥ 50% revealed a declining trend in PFS with increasing PD-L1 expression. This phenomenon was also observed in the third-generation EGFR-TKI, osimertinib [11,12], suggesting that PD-L1 expression predicts de novo resistance to EGFR-TKIs in NSCLC. Moreover, the co-occurrence of PD-L1 expression and EGFR mutations was frequently observed, with PD-L1 positivity accounting for 43.7% of 1,190 EGFR-mutant patients [1]. However, the fundamental mechanism remains unidentified.
This study aims to explore the disparities in the gene mutation spectrum between two groups of EGFR-mutant LUAD patients, those with PD-L1 ≥ 1% and<1%. Our objective is to investigate the potential mechanism of primary resistance to EGFR-TKIs in patients with co-occurring PD-L1 ≥ 1% and EGFR-mutants and to explore combination therapies that can overcome the primary resistance to EGFR-TKIs.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Study design and patients
This study was a retrospective, multicenter study conducted at three hospital centers. We recruited lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients between April 2018 and August 2022. To be eligible for this study, patients must meet the following inclusion criteria: 1) histologically and cytologically confirmed lung adenocarcinoma; 2) according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, 8th edition, stages IIIB-IV; 3) sensitizing EGFR mutation; 4) sufficient specimens to assess their PD-L1 expression. Clinical and demographic data were collected for each patient for analysis, including age, gender, smoking habits, genetic history, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG), clinical stage, baseline brain metastases, EGFR mutation, and PD-L1 status. Due to some patients not receiving subsequent treatment after testing, we recruited populations treated with EGFR-TKI monotherapy and combination therapy according to the aforementioned criteria, and analyzed their PFS. PFS was defined as the time from the first dose of EGFR-TKI to progression or death according to RECIST 1.1.
2.2. DNA extraction, target capture, and next-generation sequencing (NGS)
Genomic DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples and peripheral blood lymphocytes (PBL) using the QIAampDNA FFPE Tissue and Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Sequence libraries were created using the KAPA DNA Library Preparation Kit (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA). This library was hybridized with specially designed biotinylated oligonucleotide probes (Roche NimbleGen) targeting 1021 cancer-related genes (Supplementary Table S1). DNA sequencing was performed on Illumina HiSeq3000 Sequencing System (San Diego, CA) with paired-end reads of 2 × 100 bp.
2.3. Sequencing data analysis
Terminal adapter sequences and low-quality reads were removed from raw sequencing data. Clean reads were aligned to the GRCh37 human genome reference using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA). The Picard tool was used to mark PCR duplicates. Small insertions and deletions (InDels) and single nucleotide variations (SNVs) were called with GATK (version 3.4–46-gbc02625) and MuTect (version 1.1.4), respectively. Identify somatic copy-number variants with CONTRA (v2.0.8). Structural changes were identified using NoahCare Structural Change Detection (Intrinsic). Final candidate variants were all manually validated in the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV). Targeted capture sequencing requires a minimum average effective depth of coverage of 500× for tumor tissue and 4,000× for plasma samples [13].
2.4. PD-L1 testing and assessment of TMB
PD-L1 expression was detected by immunohistochemistry (IHC) of tumor tissues using the 22C3-PharmDx method. (Dako, Carpinteria, CA, USA). PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) was reported as the percentage of tumor cells with positive membranous staining in a slide containing at least 100 tumor-viable cells.
Tumor mutational burden (TMB) was defined as the number of somatic variants and small insertions/deletions per megabase of coding region, with a variant allele frequency (VAF)≥0.005 for ctDNA and VAF ≥ 0.03 for tumor tissue. TMB in the upper quartile (>25%) was considered high TMB (TMB-H) [14,15].
2.5. Pathogenicity analysis of mutations in DNA damage response and repair (DDR) genes
Two hundred and seventy-six genes implicated in distinct DNA damage repair pathways have been delineated as DDR genes [16]. Loss-of-function mutations (including nonsense, frameshifts, or splice junctions) in all DDR genes were classified as deleterious mutations [17]. We refer to a previously published study to determine the pathogenicity of missense mutations [18]. Patients with one (DDR+) or more deleterious DDR mutations (DRR++) were defined as DDR-positive, whereas patients without deleterious DDR mutations were defined as DDR-negative.
2.6. Mutational signature analysis
We analyzed synonymous and non-synonymous somatic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the samples, focusing on six types of base substitutions: C>A, C>G, C>T, T>A, T>C, and T>G. Based on the flanking 5’ and 3’ nucleotides of each mutated base, there were 96 possible substitution types. Using the 99 mutational signatures documented in the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC version 3) as a reference, we extracted the potential mutational signatures in each sample using the R package Mutational Patterns [19]. We then analyzed and compared the relative contributions of the various mutational signatures in both PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1% groups.
2.7. Clonality analysis for mutations
The clonality analysis method was adapted from a previous study [20], with modifications. The mutational allele frequency (MAF) was normalized by copy numbers of corresponding genes and then divided by the largest MAF within each patient, yielding the normalized Max-MAF percentage for each mutation; secondly, the frequency of each Max-MAF percentage for each mutational allele within each PD-L1 group was computed, and the probability distribution was plotted using kernel density estimation. The cutoff percentage was determined for classifying each mutation as clonal or subclonal. For EGFR mutation, we select high-frequency mutations: CTNNB1, LRP1B, PIK3CA, RBM10, RARA and TP53 along with it. The vision algorithm was then applied, identifying the first slope increase inflection point after recognizing the peak value of 0, as the cutoff of EGFR-mutated, where values ≥ cutoff as clonal, < cutoff as subclonal (Figure 5a). A similar approach was employed for other mutations, wherein the five mutations less frequent than them were selected, and the vision algorithm was applied accordingly. Finally, the distribution of different mutations within different PD-L1 statuses was analyzed by two-tailed Fisher’s exact test. To validate our algorithm and results, we additionally applied cutoffs ranging from 0.1 to 0.9 for each mutation, examining their distribution patterns and disparities (Supplementary Dataset 1&2).
2.8. Statistical analysis
To examine the differences between patient characteristics and demographic data (PD-L1 TPS ≥ 1% and TPS<1%), we used Fisher’s exact test or the chi-square test. Mann-Whitney’s U test was performed to compare the distribution of mutation number, TMB and DNA damage response and repair (DDR) status. PFS was analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared between different groups using the Log-rank test. All reported p values were two-tailed, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (20.0.0), R (4.2.1) and GraphPad Prism (8.0.2).
3. Results
3.1. Clinical characteristics of the enrolled patients
We conducted an analysis of the lung adenocarcinoma dataset across three centers, collecting 458 NSCLC patient specimens that underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) to identify EGFR gene alterations. Ultimately, 103 NSCLC patients were deemed eligible for enrollment based on the following inclusion criteria: stages IIIB-IV, tissue specimens, lung adenocarcinoma, untreated status, presence of EGFR mutation, and detection by a 1021 cancer-related gene panel. These patients were further stratified based on their PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS), with 54 patients having PD-L1 TPS < 1% and 49 patients having PD-L1 TPS ≥ 1%, and the flow chart of selection is shown in Figure 1.
The clinical characteristics of the enrolled patients are summarized in Table 1. The majority of patients in both groups were female (66.7% vs 65.3%), nonsmoking patients (61.1% vs 61.2%), and stage IV (92.6% vs 91.8%) for PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1%, respectively. In the PD-L1<1% group, the average age was 63 years old, and 11.1% had a confirmed family history of malignant tumors, while in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group, the average age was 62 years old and 8.2% had a confirmed family history. We further differentiated the types of EGFR mutations and found that EGFR L858R was more dominant in both groups (53.7% vs 44.9%), followed by EGFR Ex19del (37% vs 44.9%), with a minimal proportion of other types of mutations (9.3% vs 10.2%), for PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1%, respectively. Notably, there were no significant differences in the clinical characteristics, including age, gender, smoking status, genetic history, clinical stage, and type of EGFR mutation, between the two groups.

3.2. Mutational profile of EGFR-mutant LUAD
A total of 1127 somatic variations, including 832 single nucleotide variations (SNVs), 285 copy number variations (CNVs), and 4 structural variations (SVs), were identified from these 103 tumor samples. Figure 2(a,b) show the mutational landscape of two sets of somatic changes generated from targeted sequencing data, which showed the top 20 mutated genes considering non-synonymous somatic mutations (SNVs + INDELs). Consistent with previous studies, TP53 was the most recurrent mutant gene [21] and was identified in 33 out of 54 PD-L1<1% patients (61%) and 33 out of 49 PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients (67%). Other frequently mutated cancer genes were identified in the PD-L1 < 1% cohort, including CDKN2A (22%), CTNNB1 (13%), CDKN2B (17%), MDM2 (13%), LRP1B (11%), BRCA2 (9%), KEAP1 (9%), RARA (9%), RB1 (9%) and SMAD4 (9%), and in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort, they were MET (18%), IFNG (12%), LRP1B (12%), MLL3 (12%), PI3KCA (12%), RB1 (12%), RBM10 (10%), and TBX3 (10%).
Moreover, we observed that mutation variations of some genes exist more frequently in the PD-L1 < 1% cohort or PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort. In detail, the SMO gene alteration (nonsense and splice-site mutation) was exclusively identified in 4 of 49 PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients and showed a significant difference compared with that of PD-L1<1% patients (PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1%, 0% vs. 8%; p = 0.048) (Figure 3(a)). Meanwhile, except for EGFR, the most frequent CNV changes in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort was MET amplification (18.4%), followed by MYC amplification (16.3%), SDHA amplification (12.2%), and IFNG amplification (12.2%). In the PD-L1<1% cohort was CDKN2A deletion (20.4%), CDKN2B deletion (16.7%), and MYC amplification (16.7%). CNV differential analysis revealed significant MET amplification between the two groups, with higher copy number gain observed in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group (PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1%, 7% vs. 18%; p = 0.023). However, there were no significant differences in the frequency of CDKN2A/2B homologous deletion between the PD-L1<1% tumors and positive tumors (16.7% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.128) (Figure 3(b)). In addition to comparing mutation frequencies, we analyzed somatic alteration interactions. Co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity analyses unveiled significant associations in SMO with NSD1 and RBM10; FAT1 with CREBBP and RBM10; ERBB4-PI3KCA; ATM-GRIN2A, showing notable co-occurrence patterns in PD-L1 ≥ 1%. Additionally, SMARCA4-KEAP1, PALB2-BRCA2, FAT1-LRP1B, ZFHX3 with KEAP1 and SMARCA4, exhibited significant co-occurrence in PD-L1<1%. Nevertheless, neither group revealed significant mutually exclusive genes (Figure 3(c)).
Based on the co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity analysis, we identified genes that co-mutated in PD-L1 ≥ 1% negative cases. Among these, the TP53-PIK3CA showed a trend toward significance (PD-L1 ≥ 1% and PD-L1<1%, 12.2% vs. 1.9%; p = 0.051) (Supplementary Figure S2a). Concurrently, we performed examination of oncoplot high-frequency mutation gene combinations to identify meaningful co-mutation patterns (Figure 3(d)).
Upon analyzing the mutation features in the two groups, we observed that missense mutations constituted the most prevalent variant, followed by in-frame deletion or nonsense mutation (Supplementary Figure S1 a-b). Further analysis examination revealed that the number of genome variations detected in each patient was similar between PD-L1<1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1% groups. Analysis classification includes the combination of SNVs and CNVs, CNV amplification or deletion, and CNV counts. Despite consistent results above, indicating that PD-L1-positive tumors have fewer altered genes compared to PD-L1-negative tumors, these differences did not reach statistical significance level (Supplementary Figure S1 c-f).
PD-L1 expression has limited predictive value for immunotherapy response in EGFR-mutated lung cancer. Evaluating Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB) and DNA Damage Response and Repair (DDR) gene alterations alongside PD-L1 expression may provide insights into primary TKI resistance [18,22]. DDR gene alterations can also predict chemotherapy sensitivity [23], especially to platinum-based chemotherapy [24,25]. The DDR-positive ratio exhibited a trend toward greater prevalence in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort (DDR+/DDR++: 77.6% vs. 66.7%; DDR+: 57.1% vs. 44.5%) (Figure 3(e–f)), although no statistically significant difference is presently observed between the groups.
The median TMB in PD-L1 ≥ 1% group was 3.84 (range, 0.96–30.72) mutations/Mb, and the TMBs for the 25th and 75th percentiles were 1.92 and 5.76, respectively. Classification of tumors into high and low groups based on the 25th percentile of TMB and 8 patients (8/54, 14.8%) had high TMB. The median TMB in PD-L1<1% group (3.84 mutations/Mb; range, 0.00–49.00) was similar to the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group (p = 0.998), and there was no significant difference in the proportion of patients with high TMB between the two groups (13.3% vs. 14.8%, p = 0.82) (Supplementary Figure S2 b-c).
Overall, patients with EGFR mutations showed lower TMB regardless of PD-L1 expression, which is consistent with previous reports [1,26].
3.3. Mutational signature analysis
Mutational signatures provide insights into past endogenous (such as DNA damage, repair and replication) and exogenous mutagenic processes and were associated with clinical features, including survival rates and treatment response. When comparing the mutational patterns between PD-L1 < 1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1% NSCLC patients, a total of six single Base Substitution (SBS) signatures (corresponding to COSMIC signatures) were extracted from all samples. They were SBS42 (Occupational exposure to haloalkanes), SBS39 (Unknown), SBS31 (Prior chemotherapy treatment with platinum drugs), SBS24 (Aflatoxin exposure), SBS23 (Unknown), and SBS7b (UV exposure), respectively (Figure 4(a)). When comparing mutational signatures between the two cohorts, signature SBS42 was markedly more common in the PD-L1<1% group (p = 0.006), implying this population had higher exposure to haloalkanes (Figure 4(b)). Conversely, signature SBS31 was substantially more prevalent among the PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients (p = 0.05), indicating they may exhibit an enhanced DNA damage by platinum-based chemotherapy (Figure 4(c)). We further analyzed signatures for small insertions and deletions (ID); however, no significant ID signatures were observed.
3.4. Functional enrichment of somatically mutated genes by GO and KEGG analysis
To elucidate the potential roles of these somatic alteration genes, we investigated the associated biological processes (BP) and signaling pathways through GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis using the R package cluster Profiler (version 4.6.2). This analysis was performed to obtain gene set enrichment results influenced by the number of distinct SNVs/CNVs mutations between the two groups. In GO enrichment analysis, compared with the PD-L1<1% group, the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group shows differential mutations mainly enriching in the cohort was response and recombination of DNA damage pathways, the transition from G1 to S phases in the cell cycle, and regulation of ERK1 and ERK2 cascades (Figure 4(d)).
As illustrated in Figure 4(e), both the PD-L1 < 1% and PD-L1 ≥ 1% groups exhibited significantly pronounced enrichment in the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway, as indicated by KEGG analysis. This pathway plays a key role in mediating cell proliferation and apoptosis following EGFR activation. Consistent with the EGFR-TKI resistance mechanism, the Jak-STAT and FoxO signaling pathways were more likely to be enriched in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group. In contrast, the MAPK and Rap1 signaling pathways appeared to be more enriched in the PD-L1 < 1% group. These findings suggest the complexity of EGFR-TKI resistance mechanisms. Additionally, we observed that adaptive immune response and NF-kappa B signaling were unique to the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group.
3.5. Analysis of dual clonal status in egfr-mutant
Drug resistance was strongly associated with intra-tumoral heterogeneity. Hence, we evaluated the possible correlation between tumor clonality and PD-L1 status in EGFR-mutant patients by examining the driver genomic alterations in the genetic abnormalities found in 103 NSCLC patients. We determined the cutoff by algorithm, for categorizing each driver mutation gene as clonal or subclonal based on the percentage of normalized Mutant Allele Frequency (MAF), focusing the cutoff value of 0.6 for EGFR mutation (Figure 5(a)). Then, evaluating the frequency distribution of clonal/subclonal alterations between PD-L1 ≥ 1% and PD-L1<1% groups. In PD-L1<1% samples with mutations in RARA and PIK3CA, clonal alterations were observed more frequently compared to samples with PD-L1 ≥ 1% (Figure 5(b,c), Supplementary Dataset 2, frequency of clonal alteration in PD-L1<1% group, respectively: 4.92% (6/116) vs 0%, p = 0.03; 5.74% (7/115) vs 0%, p = 0.015 in PD-L1<1% group). Conversely, the TP53 clonal mutation was more concentrated in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% (Figure 5(d), Supplementary Dataset 2, 4.92% (6/116), p = 0.03).
To facilitate understanding of the relationships between multiple factors and the EGFR-TKI pathway, along with their associations with PD-L1 expression, we developed a simplified hypothetical model integrating these findings with EGFR-TKI resistance mechanisms (Figure S4).
3.6. Comparison of PFS under EGFR-TKIs combined with chemotherapy in patients with co-occurrence of PD-L1-positive and egfr-mutant
Combination therapy is a pivotal strategy to surmount EGFR-TKI resistance [27–30], and we observed an elevated frequency of DNA damage response and repair mechanisms in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group. To verify whether EGFR-TKIs combined with chemotherapy can improve the prognosis of patients with co-occurrence of PD-L1-positive and EGFR mutation, 49 patients with PD-L1 TPS<1% and 41 patients with PD-L1 TPS ≥ 1% were recruited (Table 2). The baseline characteristics of the patients, including age, gender, ECOG, brain metastases status, clinical stage, and type of EGFR mutation, with pairwise comparisons among the four groups showed no difference.

All patients were further divided into the TKI-monotherapy group and TKI combined platinum-based chemotherapy group. Taking into account the superior efficacy of third-generation EGFR-TKIs over first- and second-generation TKIs, patients included in the survival analysis are required to have received treatment with first- and second-generation TKIs, such as gefitinib, erlotinib, icotinib, afatinib, and dacomitinib, to mitigate potential biases. Patients were assessed every 6 weeks by contrast-enhanced MRI and Computed Tomography (CT) according to RECIST 1.1, between June 2018 and November 2023. The median follow-up time from the initiation of treatment to the last follow-up was 21.6 months.
The Kaplan–Meier curve for PFS in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% or negative population treated with EGFR-TKI monotherapy or combined with chemotherapy is depicted in Figure 5(e). Consistent with previous studies [6–10], our data displayed that PD-L1 ≥ 1% was associated with a significantly shorter median PFS in response to EGFR-TKI monotherapy compared with PD-L1<1% (8.6 months vs. 12.4 months, p = 0.006). However, when combined with chemotherapy, the median PFS was increased to 18.4 months for the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group, which was prolonged by 9.8 months compared with EGFR-TKI monotherapy (18.4 months vs. 8.6 months, p < 0.001). Similar trends were found in the PD-L1<1% group, the extended median PFS time was 6.2 months (18.6 months vs. 12.4 months, p = 0.039), lower than that in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group. More importantly, TKI combined chemotherapy overcame the problem of primary resistance to TKI monotherapy caused by high expression of PD-L1, as evidenced by the lack of significant difference in PFS between PD-L1 ≥ 1% and negative groups when the combination therapy was administered (18.4 months vs. 18.6 months, p = 0.606).
4. Discussion
The advent of EGFR-TKIs has transformed the therapeutic landscape for EGFR-mutated lung cancer, establishing it as the standard first-line treatment. Multiple studies have shown evidence that the PD-L1 expression contributed negatively to EGFR-TKI-induced primary resistance. Nonetheless, the exact underlying mechanisms remain elusive. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the potential mechanisms underlying PD-L1 expression that contribute to resistance to EGFR-TKI therapy. Additionally, we presented a novel therapeutic approach to overcome PD-L1 expression leading to EGFR-TKI resistance for the first time.
Regarding EGFR as the predominant gene mutation, the bulk of the mutated genes were evenly distributed. When comparing the mutation profiles in the two cohorts, it was shown that samples with PD-L1 ≥ 1% had a distinct frequency of the SMO mutation compared to those with PD-L1<1%. SMO encoded a G protein-coupled receptor that is essential in the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway. The abnormal activation of SMO and Hh signaling cascade promotes tumorigenesis by improving the tumor microenvironment, promoting angiogenesis and tumor migration in a variety of solid tumors [31,32], including NSCLC [33]. Our study did not identify significant enrichment differences in the Hh signaling pathway between the two groups, possibly due to the widespread presence of other genes involved in the Hh signaling pathway in both groups. However, this does not preclude the possibility that SMO may be one of the factors contributing to EGFR-TKI resistance mediated by PD-L1 expression. Previous studies discovered SMO gene in mediating acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs through the induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) [34,35].
The CDKN2A transcript encodes p16, a potential tumor suppressor that induces G1 cell cycle arrest by inhibiting retinoblastoma protein (Rb) phosphorylation of the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6. Inactivation of CDKN2A represents one of the most common somatic changes observed in NSCLC, involving homozygous deletion (CDKN2A/2B HD), methylation of the CDKN2A promoter and rare spot mutation [36]. In this study, CDKN2A somatic alterations included 9 (16.7%) homologous deletions, 2 (3.7%) non-homologous deletions, and 1 (1.8%) missense mutations in the PD-L1<1% cohort, while 3 (6.1%) cases of homologous deletion and 2 (4.1%) cases of missense mutation in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort. CDKN2A promoter methylation was not found in both groups. Recently, CDKN2A/2B HD was found to correlate with poor clinical outcomes in NSCLC [37,38]. While the PD-L1<1% group exhibited a higher mutation frequency of CDKN2A deletion, although no statistically significant differences were observed in CDKN2A/2B HD between the two groups.
Furthermore, a dual SMO and MET negative modulator can inhibit both Hh and MET pathways and restore the sensitivity to anti-EGFR drugs both in vitro and in vivo [39]. Earlier studies reported MET amplification incidence in the NSCLC population to range from 1% to 5% [40], without considering the PD-L1 factor. Our study results indicate that the occurrence of MET gene amplification in the PD-L1<1% group was 3.7% (2/54). In contrast, the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group exhibited a considerably elevated incidence of MET gene amplification at 18.4% (9/49). This trend has been observed in other studies as well. In a retrospective analysis [41] involving 272 NSCLC patients, MET amplification was noted in 15.1% of adenocarcinoma patients, with a notable increase in the PD-L1-positive group. MET amplification was intricately linked to PD-L1 expression. Researchers [42] have observed that 7 out of 11 (63.6%) MET-amplified NSCLC tumors exhibited PD-L1 expression in ≥1% of tumor cells. Furthermore, other studies [43,44] have added depth to this understanding by revealing a positive correlation between PD-L1 expression and MET amplification. The significantly higher proportion of MET amplification in PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients may represent a crucial factor contributing to the reduced efficacy of EGFR-TKI treatment in patients with both EGFR mutations and PD-L1 positivity.
The mechanism of PD-L1 expression leading to primary drug resistance of EGFR-TKIs has been studied before. In preclinical studies, NSCLC cell lines with EGFR mutations and high PD-L1 expression induced EMT through the activation of canonical transforming growth factor-β/SMAD signaling and reduced sensitivity to EGFR-TKIs [45]. High PD-L1 (≥1%) expression in EGFR-mutated NSCLC samples was analyzed using TCGA NCCRI dataset analysis, revealing a correlation with JAK-STAT signaling and a high mutation frequency of MUC16 [6]. This is consistent with our findings that JAK-STAT signaling and EGFR-TKI resistance signaling were more enriched in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% cohort. Despite this, we also found that in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group, mutations were more enriched in tyrosine and PIK3 phosphorylation, cell cycle G1/S phase transition, regulation of ERK1 and ERK2 cascade, and DNA recombination process. ERK1 and ERK2 were constituents of the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade signaling pathway. Upregulation of phosphorylated ERK was a widespread event in EGFR TKI-resistant NSCLC tissues and cell lines after EGFR TKI resistance developed [46]. Additionally, tyrosine and PIK3 were both involved in the resistance-associated PI3k-Akt/mTOR pathway, leading to abnormal activation [47], which was one of the reasons for EGFR-TKI resistance [48].
In Co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity analyses, the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group revealed significant co-occurrence associations, such as ATM-GRIN2A, FAR1 with CREBBP and RBM10, and so on. FAT1 was a classical tumor suppressor, and its established mechanisms involve the MAPK/ERK pathway. Meanwhile, RBM10 suppresses the activation of the PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway by downregulating Neat1_2. Additionally, CREBBP and ATM both directly regulate the DNA damage response pathway, correlated with TMB, MSI, and the level of PD-L1. ERBB4 mutation can phosphorylate Erk1/2 and Akt, both of which were effectors of the classical ErbB signaling pathway [49–52]. The co-occurrence of mutations mentioned above consistently results in poorer survival outcomes and high levels of PD-L1. In the PD-L1<1% group, ZFHX3 with KEAP1 and SMARCA4 exhibited significant co-occurrence. Previous studies have confirmed patients with ZFHX3 and KEAP1 mutations who received combined PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors with chemotherapy and exhibit positive treatment responses and longer survival. This suggests that ZFHX3 and KEAP1 mutations may serve as a potential biomarker for the immunotherapeutic benefit [53,54].
Tumor heterogeneity contributes to resistance to diseases. Intra-tumoral heterogeneity may facilitate the selection of resistant subclones, promoting the emergence of drug resistance, especially co-occurring oncogenic driver events. Therefore, we attempt to explore the association between tumor clonality and PD-L1 status in EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients by categorizing driver mutations as clonal or subclonal. Previous studies have indicated that the RARα protein interacts with PI3k on the cell membrane and functions to activate the PI3k-Akt/mTOR pathway [55,56], same for PIK3CA. Inhibiting the PI3K/mTOR signaling pathway has been shown to reduce PD-L1 levels in human NSCLC cell lines [57]. Simultaneously, TP53 mutations inhibit or lead to the non-expression of the p53 protein, also known as the tumor suppressor protein. This protein regulates the transcription of genes such as PTEN, which negatively regulates AKT kinase and mTOR, thereby controlling tumor growth and reversing the cancer phenotype [58]. In our study, we found that PD-L1<1% samples with RARA and PIK3CA mutations exhibited higher clonality, and TP53 mutations were more common being subclonal. On the contrary, in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group, RARA and PIK3CA mutations were all subclonal, and TP53 mutations were clonal, thereby potentially activating the PI3K/Akt/PTEN/mTOR pathway. These results may elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying increased resistance in PD-L1 ≥ 1% compared to PD-L1<1% groups. However, the aforementioned outcomes are only hypothetical and require validation through additional studies.
Last but not least, we examined whether EGFR-TKIs combined with platinum-based chemotherapy can benefit PD-L1 expression patients. Our study results verified that in the patients with EGFR mutation and PD-L1 ≥ 1%, EGFR-TKIs combined with platinum-based chemotherapy significantly improved median progression-free survival (PFS) compared with EGFR-TKI monotherapy, and the PFS was longer than that of the PD-L1<1% group. Several clinical studies have explored EGFR-TKIs combined with chemotherapy in the first-line treatment of patients with EGFR mutations and achieved survival benefits. In a phase II randomized clinical trial (JMIT study) [27] comparing gefitinib monotherapy and gefitinib combined with pemetrexed as first-line treatment for advanced lung cancer patients with EGFR mutations, the combination therapy group significantly prolonged PFS. In another phase III clinical trial [28], the median PFS of gefitinib plus pemetrexed and carboplatin chemotherapy (Gef+C) was significantly longer than that of the gefitinib monotherapy (Gef) group. The median overall survival (OS) was significantly prolonged with Gef+C than Gef. NEJ009 study [29] displayed that objective response rate (ORR) and PFS were better in the combination arm (gefitinib combined with pemetrexed plus carboplatin) than in the gefitinib alone arm. Median OS was also longer in the combination arm than in the gefitinib alone arm. The main reasons for limiting EGFR-TKIs plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment for patients with EGFR mutations were higher adverse effects in the combination group. Our findings provide a strategy for combination therapy optimization based on PD-L1 stratification. When PD-L1 expression was a negative biomarker that severely limits the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs monotherapy, combination chemotherapy was an urgent and feasible clinical option.
Although this study presents several findings, there are still several limitations. First, in retrospect, the results may be biased due to the limited sample size since the PD-L1 was not routinely tested until recent years. Secondly, we did not further stratify the benefit of patients with PD-L1 ≥ 50% after EGFR-TKIs combined chemotherapy due to the insufficient number of samples available for evaluation. Third, we evaluated the PFS benefit of the combination with chemotherapy. However, the long-term outcomes, including the sustainability of treatment effects and final overall survival benefits were unknown. Finally, further verification was still needed for the molecular mechanism related to the primary resistance of EGFR-TKI caused by PD-L1 expression found in this study. Therefore, more randomized clinical trials and basic studies were still needed to validate our findings.
5. Conclusion
This study highlights the crucial role of PD-L1 expression in influencing the therapeutic response of EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients to EGFR-TKI treatments. The PD-L1 ≥ 1% group exhibited distinct mutation patterns and pathway activations linked to resistance mechanisms, necessitating alternative therapeutic approaches. The combination of EGFR-TKIs with platinum-based chemotherapy significantly extended PFS, particularly in PD-L1 ≥ 1% of patients, demonstrating its potential to counteract primary resistance. These insights advocate for personalized treatment regimens integrating PD-L1 status to optimize clinical outcomes, warranting further investigation through randomized clinical trials and mechanistic studies to validate and expand these findings.

Article highlights
This study investigated the genomic characteristics and mechanisms of PD-L1-induced resistance to EGFR-TKIs in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma patients by analyzing 103 treatment-naive cases from three centers.
SMO mutations (8% vs. 0%, p = 0.048) and MET amplification (18% vs. 7%, p = 0.023) were significantly more prevalent in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group compared to the PD-L1 < 1% group.
DNA Damage Response and Repair (DDR) pathogenic mutations and pathways related to DNA recombination, cell cycle transition were more enriched in PD-L1 ≥ 1% group.
Clonal analysis revealed that RARA and PIK3CA mutations were predominantly clonal in the PD-L1 < 1% group, while TP53 mutations showed higher clonality in the PD-L1 ≥ 1% group.
The combination of EGFR-TKIs with platinum-based chemotherapy significantly improved progression-free survival in PD-L1 ≥ 1% patients (18.4 vs. 8.6 months, p < 0.001), effectively overcoming primary resistance to EGFR-TKI monotherapy.
This study provides novel insights into PD-L1-mediated EGFR-TKI resistance mechanisms and suggests a promising treatment strategy combining EGFR-TKIs with chemotherapy for patients with concurrent EGFR mutations and PD-L1 expression.
